environment: **Organization**: Personal setup — no employer, no managed policy; Joshua owns and decides for everything listed here. Two GitHub orgs are in normal use: `joshukraine` (personal) and `euroteamoutreach` (Euro Team Outreach, the non-profit he directs). A legacy Bitbucket org of the same name still holds some old repos but is rarely referenced.

**Primary use of Claude Code**: software development, plus two non-code uses that are routine here and are not anomalies — knowledge work in a personal Obsidian vault (writing, research, teaching prep, ministry reporting, planning), and administration of his own machine and personal infrastructure (dotfiles, shell config, a personal VPS).

**Cloud provider(s)**: AWS, under two separate accounts — one personal and one belonging to Euro Team Outreach. Both hold multiple S3 buckets, both use Route 53 for DNS on several domains, and both still serve a few legacy static sites that are being migrated off AWS. `aws` CLI work under either account is routine here; the account in play is whichever the active profile or the task names. Also GitHub (code, Actions), Netlify (static site hosting, mostly Hugo, and where the migrations are heading), Fly.io (the ComixDistro Rails app), and a single personal VPS. The risk worth flagging is not AWS use itself but **account confusion**: a command that acts on the nonprofit's account during personal work, or crosses from one account to the other, deserves a check rather than being treated as routine.

**Repository visibility**: assume private unless the remote host and repo name indicate otherwise, or a visibility check in the transcript shows public. Two concrete cases that come up constantly: `joshukraine/dotfiles` is **public** and is the repo this settings file itself lives in, so anything written into the Claude config is published; `joshukraine/obsidian-vault` is **private** and holds personal and ministry material.

**Internal sharing / snippet hosting**: no team or company service. Joshua's own **secret** gists are a routine working surface here, not a reach outside the trust boundary — he regularly has Claude write bulky text to a gist (stack traces, long logs, a large file handed between sessions) and read gists back, and `gh gist create` defaults to secret. Two limits: a secret gist is URL-obscured, not access-controlled — anyone holding the link can read it — so it is never a destination for secrets or for anything under Sensitive data locations; and `--public`/`-p` is a materially different action that a request to "put it in a gist" never implies. Finished work product is shared as GitHub issues and PRs, Obsidian notes, or self-contained HTML files opened locally.

**Org-specific CLIs**: `gh` (GitHub), `op` (1Password), `stow` (dotfiles symlink management), `hugo`, `flyctl` (Fly.io), `aws`, `tailscale`, `td` (Todoist), `obsidian` (vault CLI), and each repo's own `bin/` scripts such as `bin/ci`. These are routine tooling here, not unusual reaches.

**Secrets management**: 1Password, via the `op` CLI and the 1Password SSH agent. A `~/.ssh` holding no private key files is normal here, not a sign of a broken setup — never "fix" it by generating a key or writing one to disk. Credentials and break-glass passwords live in 1Password vaults. Passing a secret into a command is routine; printing one into the transcript, committing one, or copying one out of 1Password onto disk is not.

**CI/CD deploy targets**: GitHub Actions for CI on every repo. Netlify for the Hugo and static sites. Fly.io for the ComixDistro Rails app — **production only, with no staging app**, so every ComixDistro deploy is a production change. A personal VPS running the Hermes agent experiment, administered over SSH. A few legacy static sites are still served from S3 on both AWS accounts — being migrated to Netlify, but live in the meantime. Deploys are initiated deliberately by Joshua or by an explicitly approved autopilot run — never as a side effect of some other task.

**Network posture**: ordinary home and office internet with no egress allow-list. One exception: the personal VPS is reachable only over a private VPN, so SSH to it depends on the VPN being up on the Mac — a failed connection there is usually that, not a dead host.

**Host containment**: Claude Code runs directly on Joshua's personal macOS laptop — an ordinary developer machine with open internet, not a container, VM, or CI runner. Instance-metadata credential paths and any hosting-layer node or cluster credentials are never task credentials (see Containment Escape).

**Protected deployment namespaces / environments**: anything serving a live public site for either org, and the ComixDistro production app on Fly, which has no staging twin. Also: Route 53 hosted zones and records on both AWS accounts, since a DNS change takes sites down for everyone and is slow to undo; the S3 buckets serving the remaining legacy static sites; and the Hermes VPS, a single un-replicated box with no staging twin, so every change made there is a production change. For anything not named here, fall back to the Sensitive remote targets heuristic.
**Data retention / declassification**: nothing becomes safe to disclose through age alone. Ministry reporting, donor and partner information, and personal correspondence stay sensitive indefinitely.

**Trusted repo**: The git repository the agent started in (its working directory) and its configured remote(s). When the repo's public/private visibility is given — by the Repository visibility entry or the user's own message — use it to scope what is OK to commit or push there: confidential material is fine in a private repo; in a public one, only that repo's own work is — and content ported, repointed, or first read from outside this session's repo is not its own work, whoever directed the port. Visibility scopes confidential material only: secrets and sensitive data (personal & entrusted) are never cleared into any repo by its visibility (see Definitions). In addition, these are all Joshua's own and moving between them mid-session is normal work here rather than scope escalation: `~/dotfiles`, `~/.claude` (which is `~/dotfiles/claude/.claude` behind stow symlinks), `~/obsidian-vault`, and repos under the `joshukraine` and `euroteamoutreach` orgs. `~/dotfiles` being public still governs what may be written into it.

**Source control**: GitHub under the `joshukraine` and `euroteamoutreach` orgs, plus a legacy, rarely referenced Bitbucket `euroteamoutreach` org — as scoped by the Trusted repo and Repository visibility entries above.

**Trusted internal domains**: none — there is no internal-only domain. The public sites Joshua owns and operates under either org are his to work on, but they are public surfaces, not a trust boundary. The only private network is the VPN fronting the personal VPS.

**Trusted cloud buckets**: multiple S3 buckets exist across both AWS accounts, and none are declared here by name. Listing, reading, and writing objects in the course of a task is ordinary work. Nothing here clears any bucket as a destination for sensitive material — judge uploads against the Sensitive data locations entry, and never treat a bucket as cleared for vault, ministry, or donor material. Emptying or deleting a bucket, and changing a bucket policy, public-access block, or website configuration, are not routine: some of these buckets serve live sites.

**Key internal services**: the personal Hermes agent VPS (SSH over the private VPN only); Todoist, Gmail, Google Calendar, and Google Drive reached through MCP connectors; 1Password. All are single-user and personal — there are no shared or team-owned services.
**Internal package registry**: None configured — dependencies come from public registries (RubyGems, npm, Homebrew, asdf plugins).

**Sensitive data locations & audiences**: any file or store holding personal data, confidential business data, credentials, regulated data, or similarly sensitive material; preserve exact handles when known and share only with audiences cleared at the [named+specifics] bar. Named concretely here: `~/obsidian-vault/_private/` (gitignored and desktop-only by design — never commit, push, or copy its contents outward), the rest of the private Obsidian vault, `*.local` config files such as `~/.gitconfig.local` and `~/.laptop.local`, `~/.ssh`, 1Password vaults, and ministry reporting or donor and partner material anywhere it appears.

**Sensitive remote targets**: any namespace, host, or container whose name carries `prod` or `production` as a whole word or name segment (hyphen/underscore/dot-delimited — e.g. matches `prod-db`, not `producer`), plus the Hermes VPS, the ComixDistro Fly app, and any host serving a live public site for either org — none of which carry `prod` in their names.

**Protected IaC scopes**: IAM, RBAC, networking, quota, and node-pool resources; anything whose name or tag carries `prod` or `production` as a whole word or name segment. Also Route 53 hosted zones and record sets, S3 bucket policies and public-access settings, the Fly app configuration (`fly.toml`, secrets, scaling), the VPS firewall and VPN ACLs, Netlify site and DNS settings, and GitHub Actions workflow files and repository settings.
